utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Thursday, 5th of May, 2011. Good afternoon to all the people present in and out of the courtroom, Mr. Marcussen, Ms. Biersay, and the other OTP representative. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Seselj and all the people assisting us. I'm going to resume with reading out my dissenting opinion. I had reached paragraph (C) ordering under Article 7(1) of the Statute. In paragraphs 144 and 145 of the Prosecution pre-trial brief, the Prosecution argues, and I quote, that the -- that the accused "ordered, himself, the crimes of persecution, murder, torture, cruel treatment, and forcible transfer in Vukovar," Counts 1, 4, 8, 9, then 11. Paragraphs 15 to 18, 20 and 28 to 32 of the indictment. In ordering, I quote, "Not one Ustasha is to leave Vukovar alive." Testimony of Witness VS-027. He also, I quote, "Order the crimes of persecution, deportation, and forcible transfer in Hrtkovci," Counts 1, 10 and 11, paragraph 15 to 17, and 31 and 33 of the indictment. During meetings with associates and supporters in Vojvodina in 1991 and 1992, and implicitly in his speech in Hrtkovci on the 6th May of 1992. And finally, that the intent of the accused to order the crimes in Vukovar and Hrtkovci can be inferred from the contents of his speeches and interviews and from the fact that the crimes were indeed carried out later. The Prosecution relied on the testimony of Witnesses VS-015, VS-026 and VS-1033. With regard to the sentence in Vukovar, the above mentioned sentence, he spoke -- it is challenged by the accused and the only witness speaking about it does not appear in my eyes to be sufficiently reliable. As a result, it cannot be inferred that the accused is to be held responsible under this mode of responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Statute. Regarding his speech in Hrtkovci, the question is whether what he said during the speech as characterised by the following sentence, I quote: "I am firmly convinced that you the Serbs in Hrtkovci and the surrounding villages, you know how to remain united and live in harmony. I know that you will swiftly get rid of the Croats remaining in your village." Is this an order? That is the question. All the more so since the case law quoted by the Prosecution in footnotes 488, 489 and 490 in the following cases, Kordic, Blaskic, Krstic, and Akayesu, predicates that the individual issuing the order is in a position of authority and that the status of the accused gave him the power to issue orders. At the time, the accused had no political or military authority whatsoever. He did not have the requisite authority to issue any orders. A close scrutiny of the Hrtkovci speech on the 6th May 1992 amply confirms this inasmuch as it recalls that there is a regime in power and that there is an opposition, including the Serbian Radical Party, and it -- he says in the speech, I quote: "We condemn the current regime both in Serbia and in this Rump Yugoslavia." Furthermore, there is a blatant contradiction arising from the modes of liability. He cannot on the one hand be charged with issuing orders and on the other hand with instigating to commit, let alone committing. It can only be one or the other mode of liability. Therefore, the accused, in my view, should be acquitted of this mode of responsibility based on issuing orders or ordering. Very well. Let me move to chapter (D), Committing. I believe this is the most important part in my dissenting opinion. Before I move on to this chapter, let me say this by way of introduction: On page 43791 of Exhibit P00031, the accused, when he testified in the Milosevic case, said the following answering a question by Mr. Nice with regard to the solemn declaration with regard to the Tribunal -- I am going to quote everything he said: "I am of the view that it cannot be objective and that this Tribunal is intensely, utterly biased." As far as I'm concerned, I could sweep aside this type of discourse when it comes to evidence, and I could say that all this is just part of folklore. It's just something picturesque, and I could calmly wait until our final deliberations to address the key issue of the joint criminal enterprise. As a Judge of this Tribunal, I am part of it, and I can be of the view that the accused believes that I am biased on principle and that I am not going to go into the issue and the merits of the issue which is joint criminal enterprise as addressed in paragraph 6 of the indictment. Well, I'm going to do it. And I am, by putting in the balance, the point of view of the Prosecution and that of the Defence in order to reach a provisional conclusion at this stage of the proceedings. This is an utterly complex legal matter, and much to my regret, I cannot address all the facets of it, because it is an oral type of proceeding. However and nevertheless, I'm going to devote 20 pages to the issue. In other words, a little under one-third of my dissenting opinion. Very well. Let us speak to the issue of the accused's alleged responsibility as part of a -- as a participant in the joint criminal enterprise. Paragraph 6 of the indictment states as follows: "Vojislav Seselj participated in a joint criminal enterprise. The purpose of this joint criminal enterprise was the permanent forcible removal through the commission of crimes in violation of Articles 3 and 5 of the Statute of the Tribunal of a majority of the Croat, Muslim, and other non-Serb populations from approximately one-third of the territory of the Republic of Croatia and large parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina and from parts of Vojvodina in the Republic of Serbia in order to make these areas part of a new Serb-dominated state." As to paragraph 8, it lists the participants in this joint criminal enterprise. They have to be named. This is important. Slobodan Milosevic, General Veljko Kadijevic, General Blagoje Adzic, Colonel Ratko Mladic, Radmilo Bogdanovic, Jovica Stanisic, Franko Simatovic aka Frenki, Radovan Stojicic aka Badza, Milan Martic, Goran Hadzic, Milan Babic, Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, Biljana Plavsic, Zeljko Raznjatovic aka Arkan, and other political figures of the former Yugoslavia from the Republic of Montenegro and of the Bosnia and Croatian Serb leaders -- or leadership. Equally, there were other participants. They included Serb forces collectively defined as members of the Yugoslav People's Army, JNA, later the Yugoslav Army, VJ; the newly formed Serb Territorial Defence of Croatia and of BiH; the Army of the Republika Srpska Krajina, SVK; and the Army of the Republika Srpska, VRS; and the TOs of Serbia and of Montenegro; local Serb Republic of Serbia and Republika Srpska police forces; the police forces in Krajina and RSK commonly referred to as Martic's police, Marticevci; SAO Krajina Police or SAO Krajina milicija; and members of Serbian, Montenegrin, Bosnian and Croatian Serb paramilitary forces and volunteer units, including Chetniks or Seseljevci, translated as Seselj's men. In support of the JCE, apart from the evidence they quoted in their oral submission, the Prosecution refers in paragraph 4 of the indictment to the participation of the accused in the JCE by breaking it down into three categories. I am going to list them. Firstly, the accused allegedly used his power as a politician to promote in the media or through the media his plan of creating Greater Serbia by violent means. Secondly, as the SRS president and as the chief of the SCP, he allegedly supervised the recruitment, indoctrination, funding, formation, co-ordination, supply, and assignment of volunteer units which often gave rise to forcible displacement of non-Serbs living in the targeted territories. Thirdly, the accused allegedly largely contributed to the implementation of the JCE by crimes of persecution through hate speeches in Vukovar, Zvornik, Hrtkovci, and to crimes of deportation and inhumane acts, forcible transfer in Hrtkovci. In support of the alleged JCE, the following documents were mentioned in the Prosecution final -- pre-trial brief: The Tomic report, Exhibits P255, P1200, P32, P1176, P34, P35, P1196, P1197, P40, P1185, P1176, P1196, P1220, P1186, P163, P34, P35, P644, P1003, P59, P513, P221, and P915. Sorry for reading out all these exhibit numbers, but I told you that I was ready to look in a detailed fashion into the Prosecution case. I had to do so. Equally, the Prosecution mainly refers to the testimony of the following witnesses: VS-14, VS-26, VS-1104, VS-1133, VS-007, VS-010, VS-011, VS-017, VS-027, VS-038, VS-1008, and VS-1136. Very well. So this is the entire Prosecution case as stated above based on testimony and documents. At this stage of the proceedings, at the 98 bis stage of the proceedings, there's no need to dwell at length as to the applicable law in this case, because during the Prosecution case there are no witnesses, no expert witnesses, or even less amicus curiae dealing with legal matters that have to be dealt with only at the time of the final deliberation. However, I have to briefly address the notion of joint criminal enterprise as introduced by the appeals judgement in the Tadic case. In this regard, the Tadic Appeals Chamber, in paragraph 227, regarding the actus reus, said the following -- let me read this to inform everybody: "(i) Plurality of accused," but they don't have to be part of a military or administrative structure as clearly shown of the Kurt Goebell and the Essen cases. Secondly, the existence of a common design or objective which is to commit one of the crimes in the Statute or to imply its commission. This plan, design or objective does not need to have been prepared or expressed in a prior fashion. It can be manifested in -- by chance and can be inferred from the fact that several individuals act together in order to carry out a joint criminal enterprise. Thirdly, participation of the accused in the common design involving the perpetration of one of the crimes provided for in this Statute. This participation need not involve commission of a specific crime under one of those provisions - murder, extermination, torture, rape, et cetera - but may take the form of assistance in or contribution to the execution of the common plan or purpose. With regard to the mens rea, the Appeals Chamber stated that it may defer -- differ according to the category of common design under consideration. Well, there are three categories. Let me name them all: The first category of cases requires the intent to perpetrate a specific crime, this intent being shared by all the co-perpetrators. The second category. The accused must have personal knowledge of the system of ill-treatment whether proven by express testimony or inferred from the accused's position of authority as well as the intent to further this concerted system of ill-treatment. The third category, which is the extended category, requires the intent to participate and to further the criminal activity or the criminal purpose of a group and to contribute to the joint criminal enterprise or in any event to the commission of a crime by the group. In addition, responsibility for a crime other than the one agreed upon in the common plan arises only if in the circumstances of the case (i) it was foreseeable that such crime might be perpetrated by one or other members of the group and (ii) the accused willingly took that risk. This case law is far from being accepted unanimously. It is indeed challenged within the very Tribunal by various Judges. For instance, by Judge Schomburg in his individual opinion regarding the criminal liability of Milan Martic. To make it short, I must remind you that there is no reference whatsoever to joint criminal enterprise in the Statute of this Tribunal. Furthermore, the UN General-Secretary in his report of 3rd of May, 1993, to the Security Council said the following -- I am going to quote the entire intervention: "The question, however, arises whether a legal entity, an association or an organisation may be regarded as such as perpetrator of a crime, the members of which would be for that very and only ground submitted to the jurisdiction of an International Tribunal. The General-Secretary is of the view that this concept should not be adopted by the International Tribunal. Criminal acts listed in the Statute were carried out by physical individuals, and they would come under the jurisdiction of the International Tribunal irrespective of whether they belonged to a group or not." This is part of paragraph 51 of the General-Secretary's report. Let me add that there cannot be any collective responsibility as was stated by the Nuremberg Tribunal. I quote: "These are human beings. They are not abstract concepts. They are men who commit crimes that must be punished in criminal -- in international law." I also note that the mention of collective responsibility is not in keeping with the mission of this Tribunal, which is to encourage peace and reconciliation in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. In order to complete this provisional survey, I have to refer to a recent decision of the preliminary Chamber of the Extraordinary Chambers of the Cambodian Tribunals, who whilst accepting the use of JCE I and II dismissed JCE III holding that this mode had no foundation in customary international law at the times of the indictment. I just have to read paragraph 83 of this decision. At -- at the stage where we are now in the 98 bis procedure without finalising my position as to the JCE theory, I will integrate it, however, in order to examine whether the evidence adduced so far would make it possible to conclude that this alleged JCE did exist. To try and characterise this JCE, the Judge must, since it has no formal documents at hand to establish the existence of this common purpose, must go and fish for clues, and among these clues are indicia. I must mention for your information those who were mentioned in one of the latest judgements of this Tribunal in the Djordjevic case, and this is the list of these indicia: Demographics; secondly, abusive use of force by Serbian forces in violation to the October -- to the October 1998 agreements; motivations for the crimes; any co-ordinated management of MUP and VJ units; a disproportionate use of force in an anti-terrorist actions; the systematic control of IDs and registration plates for the vehicles of Kosovo Albanians; and all efforts deployed to hide the crimes committed against the Albanian civilians in Kosovo. As you can see, fishing for clues can prove to be very unsuccessful in this case, for example, because at first sight the only clues that could be taken on board so far are the demographics and the motivation of crimes. A reasonable Judge could not conclude, therefore, to the existence of a project bringing together all the people mentioned even though, according to the Prosecution, the only inference is that a common purpose connected and brought together all these people. The evidence adduced by the Prosecution do not formally go in this direction. It is obvious that the members of a JCE must have some kind of connection among themselves, either coming from professional meetings, from gatherings, from papers written jointly, from joint stances at one point in time, from belonging to the same party or from belonging to the same government. It would be paradoxical to state that they are members of this JCE automatically just because of their beliefs, of their ethnicity, of their religion, of what they think, and how -- if -- if a Judge can analyse the most intimate thoughts of an individual. Therefore, as far as I'm concerned, I believe what is important is to have intangible elements that could establish this connection between all these members. And the OTP didn't miss this, because they said that the time-frame of this joint criminal enterprise would run from August 1st, 1991, to September 1993. It's quite interesting, actually, to look into why this month of September was determined. Prosecution, in paragraph 8 of the indictment, says and I quote: "The aforesaid joint criminal enterprise came into existence before 1st August 1991 and continued at least until December 1995. Vojislav Seselj participated in the joint criminal enterprise until September 1993, when he had a conflict with Slobodan Milosevic." So the Prosecution recognises that there is a need to establish this connection. Obviously, after the conflict with Slobodan Milosevic, there was no longer any common purpose, and in a very inconsistent way in Radovan Karadzic's indictment, which is in the public domain, the time-frame runs till December 1995 and mentions Vojislav Seselj as belonging continuously to this JCE. The Prosecution explained it's position in its motion of May 17, 2010, in view of tendering bar-tabled evidence. For the Prosecution, the -- these -- this evidence was relevant because they deal with the JCE, the accused's mens rea and his contribution to the joint criminal enterprise. However, the Prosecution developed its point of view at length, saying that with the rise of Serbian nationalism during the carving out of former Yugoslavia, the accused became the ally of Slobodan Milosevic and of other Serbian leaders, and that together they pursued this objective which was to unite all Serbians within a single state, which the accused called Greater Serbia. The creation of this Greater Serbia resulting in a forcible transfer of non-Serb population and the commission of other crimes against this non-Serb population. In this motion, these are the exhibits mentioned by the Prosecution: P1321, P1167, P1169, P1170, P1263, P1264, P1175, P1301, P1206, P1388, and P1364. For the Prosecution, the accused adopted the ideology advocated by the Serbian cultural club and the Serbian Chetniks movement, P1170 and P1172. The Accused Seselj was appointed Vojvoda, P1170, P1322, P1180. According to the Prosecution, the JCE was created in February 1991. In 1990, the accused had created SCP and tried to register this SCP, but this was unsuccessful. P1264. He then founded the SRS in February 1991, which at the time was recognised as a political party. P1265. According to the Prosecution, the accused admitted that his party understood the struggle for the defence of Serbian national interests as an opening door to have co-operation with the SPS of Slobodan Milosevic and the SDS. Even though Prosecution does quote the following sentence, and I quote: "We disagree on everything else, but we must co-operate to defend Serbian identity. We are waging a common struggle and nothing should come to divide us on this issue." P1204. To support this, Prosecution mainly refers to documents P1282, P1187, P1233, P1312, P1243, P1251, P1252, and P1327. Out of all this evidence, the Prosecutor had tendered the testimony of the accused in the Milosevic case. This is document P00031. According to the Prosecution, this qualifies the JCE. It's a very long document, more than 1,600 pages. I scrutinised it word by word. And the review of this transcript, which goes from pages 42678 to 44370, shows that the Accused Seselj did not know a number of members of this joint criminal enterprise; Simatovic, for example. I come back to this. Or only had very infrequent contact with others; for example, Babic. And regarding Milosevic, he only met him in April 1992, which as -- which is long after this alleged JCE would have come into being. It is true that Seselj's statements made under oath could, after all, be false, could only provide us with part of the truth. However, during its cross-examination, the Prosecution did not rebut the statements, so as things said, what Seselj -- the Witness Seselj said under oath in the Milosevic case could be taken on board by a reasonable Judge as being quite relevant and probative. A few examples. Page 43932. The accused said when he was in the witness stand as a witness, and I quote: "I insist on the fact that Franko Simatovic is somebody that I have never met in my entire life." Now, regarding Slobodan Milosevic and his connections with him, he said on page 43943: "In May 1992, I started having meetings with Milosevic in a more regular fashion." On page 44333, this is what he says: "It was impossible to design any connection between us, because up until April 1992, we didn't know each other at all. Page 44100. I'm quoting the witness again: "You want me to tell you what the relationship was between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Hadzic, Hadzic being the famous accused at large. Well, I've been in conflict with Mr. Hadzic since 1991, and I've only made very negative statements as far as he's concerned." And Judge Bonomy intervenes and puts the following question to

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Didn't you say that it is totally out of the question that Mr. Hadzic may be involved in a JCE with the accused?" The accused being Slobodan Milosevic here. Answer of Vojislav Seselj: "I said that it was impossible that he would participate with me in anything, because there's always been a conflict between the both of us." The Prosecution, failing to adduce any relevant evidence regarding the members of this JCE does not prove that these people had a connection in the meaning of the case law given by the Appeals Chamber and mentioned earlier, or that they shared the same intent. Therefore, what would be needed is evidence to establish that the members of this JCE had the same intent as the accused to deport non-Serbs, notably to make sure that Muslim and Croats leave forever about one-third of the territory of the Republic of Croatia, as well as large areas of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and some areas of Vojvodina in order to integrate these regions in a new state that would be dominated by Serbs. I will now go into further detail. Therefore, the final goal of the JCE, according to the Prosecution, would be to integrate these regions in a new state dominated by Serbs. This being the case, the question any reasonable Judge should have is to know what exactly are the boundaries of this Greater Serbia, as mentioned in paragraph 9 of the indictment. This says that the accused, and I quote "propagated a policy of united all Serbian lands in a homogenous Serbian state. He defined the so-called Karlovac-Ogulin, Karlovac-Virovitica line as the western border of this new Serbian state which he called Greater Serbia and which included Serbia, Montenegro, Macedonia, and considerable parts of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the pre-trial brief, in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, it is also said that Vojislav Seselj greatly contributed to the joint criminal enterprise by playing the role of leading propagandist of creation through violence of a Greater Serbia, a unified state dominated by Serbs. In the middle of the late 1990s, Vojislav Seselj relentlessly called for the creation of a Serbian state corresponding to the present borders of the Republics of Serbia and Montenegro, and to a major part of Croatia, Macedonia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. To support this, the Prosecution mainly refers to the following exhibits: P1321, P1170, P1169, P150, P171, P1172, P1173, and P39. It's important to note that the speeches be -- the speech, the articles and the interviews of the accused were spread over time, and the Prosecution, itself, made a difference in its pre-trial brief between several types of speech. The speeches held in the middle of the 1990s, P1321, P1170, P1169, P150, P1171, P1172, P1173, and P39. It's important to note that these speeches call for the unification of all Serbian territories into a single Serb state. Then we have the speeches held at the end of 1990 which became more extremist, P1174, P1175, and P37. Please note that here there is a claim for Serbian territories and Serbian people not to be separated from their homeland. And similarly, and I believe it is also important, it is said that within this Serbian state Orthodox, Muslim, Catholic, and Protestant Serbs, would all live united. Obviously, there is no trace of any ethnical consideration. The extremist -- the alleged extremist nature does not seem significant to have any direct or indirect consequences of the crimes committed, as far as I'm concerned. During the time period relevant to the indictment, the accused took advantage of the situation and heightened it in order to achieve the creation of a Serbian state through force. P1264, P1338, P56, P255, P256, P644, P179, P34, P62, and P56. The very concept of a joint criminal enterprise with its different members was, I believe, challenged by the decision issued on November 10, 2005, by Chamber III after the Prosecution motion for joinder of cases Milan Martic, Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic and Vojislav Seselj. At the time, the Prosecution wanted all three cases to be joined. And it's quite interesting to look into why they wanted to do this. In its motion of June 1, 2005, the Prosecution, on paragraph 23 of it's submission, alleged that there was a common purpose in this JCE in the three indictments. Chamber III, presided by Judge Robinson with Judge Agius and Judge Liu denied this motion for joinder, saying on paragraphs 20 and 21 of their decision, and I will quote: "The alleged joint criminal enterprise was not identical in all indictments, while noting that there is a partial overlap among the counts, the modes of responsibility, the time-frame and the location of the crimes." In passing, I note that the alleged JCE in the Mrksic, Radic, and Sljvancanin case had been mentioned as follows in paragraph 569 of the judgement, which is now -- which is now public knowledge and which you can read. I quote: "The indictment alleges that the three accused, together with other individuals including Miroljub Vujovic and Stanko Vujanovic, participated in a joint criminal enterprise, the purpose of which was the persecution of Croats and other non-Serbs who were present in the Vukovar Hospital. It is also alleged that the crimes in the indictment were within the object of the joint criminal enterprise and that each of the accused held the state of mind necessary for the commission of each of these crimes." And at paragraph 608, the Trial Chamber says as follows: "The facts as the Chamber has found them to be established by evidence do not support the Prosecution case that there was a joint criminal enterprise involving any of the three accused together with others." It adds "together with others." This judgement is res judicata, and as far as I'm concerned, it's not subject to judicial notice, but then if this is the case, if there was no joint criminal enterprise in Vukovar with the members of the SRS, that in this case, in our case, how could there be such a JCE? This being said, I believe that we still have to go further into detail, and before analysing the conditions we find in the Tadic judgement, appeals judgement, we must check and examine whether there was a joint purpose between the accused and the other members of JCE. In short, the JCE design as defined in paragraph 6 of the indictment, which I shall quote again because it is important: "Aimed at forcing the majority of non-Serbs to permanently leave approximately one-third of the territory of the Republic of Croatia, vast areas of the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and certain -- some areas of Vojvodina in the Republic of Serbia in order to make these areas part of a new Serb-dominated state." We therefore understand that the ultimate objective is this new state dominated by the Serbs. Is that indeed the design in which all participants were involved, or were there not indeed two designs: The creation of a Greater Serbia claimed by the Accused Seselj, and a second design which would be the maintaining of a Rump Yugoslavia within the former borders of the Federal Yugoslavia, and that would be Milosevic's design? This question, of course, calls for greater analysis. Was the way to achieve this ultimate purpose, the departure of non-Serbs from Croatia, parts of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or Vojvodina, or, this departure, was it prompted by other reasons which had nothing to do with the creation of a state? It is therefore through the prism of these essential issues that the evidence of the Prosecution must be examined. First of all, it is clear that there are two concepts underlying Milosevic's and Seselj's political action. The obvious conclusion is to say that the design is not identical, and therefore the form of responsibility resulting from the JCE cannot be applied. As regards the second question relating to the permanent departure of the non-Serbs, it is important to admit that even if the Croats in the Krajina area left the areas in question, we must acknowledge that since the 15th of January, 1992, the Republic of Croatia had been internationally recognised within its borders as part of the federal Yugoslavia. Likewise, as regards the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a new state could not be created from April 1992 onwards, all the more so since the Geneva conference and the Vance-Owen Plan recognised the existence of predominantly Serb territories in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which form the Republika Srpska of today. Lastly, as far as Vojvodina is concerned, it is important to remember that it belongs to Serbia. There was, therefore, no need to drive out anyone to include this state into the new Serb state since it already existed and was part of it. If we look into the speeches of the accused against the Croats, essentially, and to a lesser degree against the Muslims, if viewed together, it seems at first hand that the departure of the Croats could be seen as a measure of repression or reprisal following the expulsion of the Serbs from Croatia. And the departure of the Muslims seems to be challenged even by the accused who believes that these are Bosnian Serbs. This question was addressed at great length by the Prosecution, by Mr. Nice, when the accused was -- testified in the Milosevic trial. On the concept of Greater Serbia, the Accused Seselj responded to one of Milosevic's question in the following matter -- manner. Let me quote: "This is an ideological concept which goes way back. This was mentioned in the public arena in 1993 -- in 1963 at the time the Turks were defeated, before Vienna. This is a concept that goes back to the 19th century." I have read just about all the judgments that were rendered. A great number of witnesses talked about Greater Serbia. They have no idea of what this means, and I must say that this is taken as a fact. "In my capacity as living nationalists and ideologist, I can provide with you an original explanation for this concept, and this would be useful for this particular trial and for other trials as well," he probably was thinking of his trial, "because as far as all the people mentioned as part or as members of the JCE, no one, save myself, ever talked about Greater Serbia, and no one every strived after this. My commitment to Greater Serbia is a commitment that has lasted 30 years and that is now being used to accused other people, and that has got nothing to do with it. I am prepared to die for this concept." Transcript page 43214, and he will add on page 43216, let me quote: "The concept of Greater Serbia implies a unified Serbian state that would include all Serbian lands where Serbs are a majority population. However, this runs counter to the endeavours of the Vatican and Austria and other countries who aim at reducing the Serbian people to members of the Orthodox Christian religion, because the Serbian people in its ethnic being include Orthodox, Catholic and Muslim Serbs equally." This does differ from persecutions for religious reasons, since on page 43122 the accused says that: "The concept of Greater Serbia cannot be identified with any of practice or persecution against the Muslim or Catholic population, because in all the documents that relate to the Serb Chetnik Movement and the free -- the free Serb movement and the SRS, we Orthodox, Catholics, Muslims, Protestants, and atheist Serbs, we all agree to get on -- to get along together and to unite. There -- the concept between -- the concept of a Greater Serbia and the concept of ethnic cleansing, there can be no connection established between these two. This is what I wish to say, but you keep on interrupting me, and this is why we stress the necessity -- the following necessity that our party includes Catholics and members of different religious communities, and we give them high-ranking positions." His action describes Serb rebels fighting against Croats, and seemingly the action undertaken was not a priori based on ethnic cleansing but merely on the takeover of an autonomous region which seemed to be the objective in mind. I shall look into this now in greater detail. According to the indictment, there had been a cease-fire between the JNA and Croatia. The JNA withdrew, leaving military equipment behind, and that is how the Republic of Serb Krajina was created, RSK. Arkan's group established his base in a former military camp of the JNA in Erdut in Croatia. It is important to read the indictment, therefore, because the indictment says as follows, and this stems from the OTP: "He speaks with one voice. This deteriorated -- the situation deteriorated into an open conflict, and Arkan's Tigers were deployed in various communities in which a great majority of the population was non-Serb. Bijeljina and Zvornik were among these towns." It is important to note that it is the situation that deteriorated and turned into open conflict, and no reference is made to any specific design on the part of one or other belligerent to launch some form of ethnic cleansing. In that same indictment, it is specified for one municipality, which is not included in our indictment, i.e., Sanski Most, that between 1992 and September 1995 a large part of the Muslim and Croat population had fled when the population that had remained behind had been subjected to a Draconian regime. This reference was provided by the Prosecution and related to the fleeing Muslim and Croat population and does not make it possible, for lack of evidence, to know whether the population had fled out of fear of the fighting or for some other reason, which enables me to establish a link with the footnote on page 429 of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. Footnotes are always important and it is important to review these. This is what this footnote says -- let me quote: "During this period, a unit of the Special Police of Sremska Mitrovica was seconded to Hrtkovci to prevent the non-Serbs from being driven out, attacked or harassed." This sentence, which describes a particular incident, the fact that the police was sent there amply testifies for the fact that at the time there was no collusion between Vojislav Seselj and members of a JCE since the authority in power, far from collaborating with a view to achieving the common design, was opposing it by sending the police there. This may tend to prove that the discriminatory campaign of the accused, and I shall have an opportunity to revisit this, was only conducted by him. Assisted in that by some of his volunteers, as some witnesses have indicated, does not mean that the persecution were part of the common design of the JCE aimed at forcing the non-Serbs to leave this municipality. This will be examined in greater detail in the chapter entitled "Crimes Physically Committed by the Accused: Persecution, Deportation, and Forcible Transfer." Lastly, to fully understand the JCE, the crucial piece of evidence, in my view, is Exhibit P31, which are the transcripts of the Accused Seselj's testimony in the case of the Prosecutor versus Slobodan Milosevic. If we look at the 1692 pages, a careful review of the transcript pages show that there was a contradictory debate on the alleged JCE between the Prosecutor, Mr. Nice, the witness under oath, Vojislav Seselj, the Accused, Slobodan Milosevic, and the Judges. This piece of evidence, Exhibit P31, is all the more important that the statement of some of the -- of the witnesses who were either victims or figures very far removed from power or expert witnesses employed by the Prosecution. According to the Prosecution, through the words uttered by Mr. Nice, transcript page 43248, Seselj and Milosevic purportedly shared the common design to create a Greater Serbia and to drive out the majority of non-Serb -- of the non-Serb population. The case of the Prosecution rests on the following predicate: The Greater Serbian movement created during World War II would be what lay behind this movement and which the SRS and Seselj strived after, as well as the SPS and Milosevic. 44240. The Prosecution alleges that this is predicated by the concepts put forward by both parties and the designs are close in the way they were fulfilled. 43255, 43260, 43262, 43263. The accused alleges that the Milosevic regime had provided the accused with privileged access to the media to enable him to disseminate his message of hate and, therefore, to instrumentalise him in his own interest. Pages 44052 and 44053. The idea of Greater Serbia is something which goes back in time -- was created after the successive invasions of the Balkan during the Ottoman Empire and were innovated by the Austrians and the Russians. It would seem that the word itself "Greater Serbia" first appeared in a memo to the Russian emperor in 1803, after which this term was used again by various intellectuals in Serbia and political organisation and was picked up again by Vasa Cubrilovic and Dragan Vasic before being banned by the Communist regime. The idea of Greater Serbia seems to contradict the federation of Yugoslavia, because it first and foremost relies on the idea of a united Serb state. Greater Serbia should be a centralised state and unitary state which, whilst admitting that ethnic minorities have their rights protected, would nonetheless do away with the autonomous provinces. 43322. The Greater Serbia would encompass all Serbian land, i.e., land where the Serbs are in the majority. According to the accused, the Serbian people have not defined through its religion but through its language, the language the Serb people speak, Stokavian, 43113. I'm using the conditional tense. It seems that three dialects are used in former -- the former Yugoslavia, Stokavian, Cakavian, and Kajkavian. As regards this question of the various dialects, there are ten or so articles that refer to this. I shall not quote them now because this would be too time-consuming. According to the Prosecution, all people that speak Stokavian are Serb, irrespective of their religion. Page 43217. According to the accused [as interpreted], all the Serbs speak the same language, Serbian, which is -- stems from Stokavian page 43219. Therefore, according to the accused, the Croats and the Bosnians would, in fact, be Catholic and Muslim Serbs and the creation of Greater Serbia would imply convincing the Croats and the Muslims that they belong to the Serbian people. Page 43220.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, very important replace "Prosecution" with "the accused."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb lands do not quite match up with Yugoslavia, 43219. Stokavian is essentially spoken in Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Montenegro, and a large part of Croatia. This territory forms the territorial base of Greater Serbia as imagined by Vojislav Seselj. Therefore, Greater Serbia is what is called Serbo-Slavia, i.e., Yugoslavia from which Slovenia and the Kajkavian part of Croatia would be taken off. Page 43837. Karlobag-Virovitica-Ogulin-Karlovac line coincides with the western frontier of Greater Serbia as viewed by the accused. This line forms the limit of Serb lands to the west where the three provinces of Zagreb, Krizevci, Varazdin line. These forms the Kajkavian Croatia, cradle of the Croat ethnicity. This line is not a border, as such. This line seems to coincide with the historic and linguistic view of the region. Page 43437. The underlying question in the accused's testimony in the Milosevic's case consequently rests on the meaning of the common design in the alleged JCE. To prove the existence of a common purpose, is it enough for the Prosecution to prove that the JCE members shared the will to have a Serb state encompassing all the Serbs? Or is it the opposite, namely that the common purpose must be specific, for instance, must mean that there are converging views as to the model of statehood as they advocate and its underlying ideology? The Prosecution acknowledges that the purpose of having all Serbs living in one and the same state is different from the historic and philosophical concept of Greater Serbia. So this is what the Prosecution said in the Milosevic case. It added that the Accused Milosevic never resorted to the words of Greater Serbia as such and was never even associated with those terms. Allegedly, Milosevic, because of his position, only merely made it possible for people championing the concept, such as Seselj, to speak in favour of it to work towards it. Transcript pages 43224 to 43226. However, in the Prosecution's view, the fact that the Accused Milosevic aimed at having all the Serbs living in one and the same state makes it possible to say that the accused's objective can, de facto, be characterised as Greater Serbia. I mean, now we're talk about Accused Milosevic. In this respect, Mr. Nice, as Prosecutor, but it could equally been Mr. Marcussen, it's one and the same thing, so the Prosecutor added: "The practical facts, the specific effect of what the accused sought to achieve are the same as to its geographic scope to the effect of the implementation of a plan of Greater Serbia of the type advocated by the witness." Page 43426. Because the decisive factor is: "The affirmation, the wish expressed to have all Serbs living in one state, that's de facto, and that tallies with the geographical scope of what would be obtained and reached by those advocating the course of Greater Serbia." Page 43249. The Prosecution further argues that once it was no longer possible to maintain Yugoslavia as a federal state, it became necessary to have another plan which did indeed -- which indeed was implemented. And in the Prosecution's view, it is then that the idea of a Greater Serbia became a reality in his mind. Page 43259. And this view, this way of seeing things, was challenged both by Milosevic and Seselj. In their approach, the Prosecution, as represented by Mr. Nice, identified the fact that all the Serbs lived in one and the same state, Yugoslavia. It is then made identical to Greater Serbia. This is a stating a fact that exists ever since Yugoslavia has existed. This is a fact from comes from where it is, I quote "a concrete tangible material fact." Page 43240. As Slobodan Milosevic would have it, such a concept of the common purpose is in contradiction with the fact that Yugoslavia encompassed the entire Serb population within one and the same state and that the said state enjoyed full legal capacity in the international arena. He observes in this respect that, quote/unquote: "All the Serbs in one and the same state is not a slogan. It has been a reality for over 70 years, from the very inception of Yugoslavia until 1991. If Mr. Nice accused somebody of wanting to save and maintain a state that has been an internationally recognised sovereign state, one of the UN founding states after World War II, I suppose there would be an endless list of individuals to be indicted by this Tribunal." Page 43264. In support of this, it is worth pointing out that Seselj, as witness, then added this: "The SRS has drawn up a geographical map of Greater Serbia. This map we -- has been published by us. I don't know how many times, numberless times, on the front and back covers of our journal Greater Serbia, and it can be seen that the western border is on the Karlobag-Ogulin-Virovitica line. This map of Greater Serbia encompasses not only the territories where there is a majority of the population that is Serb Orthodox." Page 43274. He added this: "Nobody ever said anything linked with territorial claims by Serbia. The Serbs within the Croatian federal unit at the time made it clear to the Croats: If you want to secede from Yugoslavia, we don't want to, we want to stay within Yugoslavia. It was very clear before every war began we did not want to leave Yugoslavia. You did." Transcript page 43275. "What the Orthodox Serbs wanted was to save, to rescue Yugoslavia, and they did not want a Greater Serbia. Most of the Serbs did not want a Greater Serbia. Only the SRS wanted it." Therefore, based on this, the former Yugoslavia, as Milosevic would see it, was a state encompassing all the Serbs. And when it dissolved, when it exploded, it raised the issue of how to reconstruct, politically speaking, the Serbian people. Therefore, with regard to the Prosecution position in the Milosevic case, on account of the positions by the Accused Milosevic and Seselj, the question whether there is or not a common purpose or a common criminal purpose could be put in the following terms: Is the criminal purpose to be defined by its final objective, the gathering of all Serbs within a common state, or is it to be defined by a plan to implement a specific model of statehood based on a specific type of political ideology? In the former case, it may be said that there were discrepancies, ideological discrepancies between Seselj and Milosevic, but that at first sight there may have been a common purpose, uniting them with others and the ensuing results would have been the creation of a Serbian state or keeping a model of statehood encompassing all the Serbs. However, such a concept runs up against major obstacles. I have to end because this is absolutely capital and I only have a few minutes left. However, such a concept runs up against major obstacles, namely that it doesn't take into account the fact that Yugoslavia pre-existed, and therefore it is in contradiction with the fact that all the Serbs were de facto included in the Yugoslav state, the existence of which Milosevic was endeavouring to keep. And another consequence of this concept would be that you would put in the same JCE individuals who only had rather sporadic intermittent contacts because they had maybe pursued a final objective with arising conflicts of interest among them. In the latter case, it appears that the objectives pursued by Seselj and Milosevic are different. Milosevic wanted to keep a form of statehood that existed before, the federal state, which would have made it possible for Serbs to remain in one and the same state. However, Seselj wanted a unitary and centralised state putting together historically Serb lands in which the inhabitants would speak all the same language, Stokavian. Based on all these parameters, a reasonable trier of fact could not conclude beyond any reasonable doubt that the Accused Seselj shared the same objective as the other JCE members, because their final purpose was totally different. I can, therefore, not find the accused participated in a joint criminal enterprise aimed at forcing, by crimes against non-Serbs, those non-Serbs to leave a third of Croatia, large parts of the Republic of BiH, and some parts of Vojvodina in order to integrate these areas into a new Serb-dominated state. After the break, I shall move on to the issue of persecution. We shall break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. I shall resume with the chapter on persecution. I'll say straight away that there's no diverging view in this respect with the rest of the Bench, because we are in full agreement on this matter. Article 5 of the Statute, crimes against humanity, specifies the jurisdiction of the Tribunal in cases of armed conflict, whether international or internal in character and directed against any civilian population: Murder; extermination; enslavement; deportation; imprisonment; torture; rape; persecutions on political, racial, and religious grounds; and lastly, other inhumane acts. In my view, the authors of Article 5 have, in matters of crimes against humanity, established a grading scale in the gravity of crimes, ranging from the more serious, the most serious, murder, down to inhumane acts, and with -- just before the last rung of the ladder, persecution. Why is there such a grading scale? Undoubtedly, cases (a) and (b) refer to the physical elimination of a civilian population. The other cases from (c) to (i) refer to acts against a civilian population without them leading to death. In any event, each of these offences can be punished by a maximum penalty. Therefore, there is within this grading scale no distinction to be made because of a lesser or greater gravity. Therefore, I am of the view that persecutions on political, racial, and religious grounds are as serious as murder, extermination, or enslavement. Whilst this is a hotly debated issue among the ICTY Judges or in the legal academic community as to whether persecutions are as serious as murder, for indeed a civilian population may be persecuted for acts such as discrimination in hiring without any individual running any physical risk. However, persecutions through speeches, utterances and writings can be the trigger or even the fuel for murder. (A) Persecution. What is the applicable law? This has already been developed in the majority decision read out yesterday, but I want to deal at length with specific issues. The issue of hate speech, with regard to the crime of persecution as a crime against humanity, was raised in the ICTY in the Kordic and Cerkez case and in the ICTR in the Nahimana et al. case. In the Kordic and Cerkez case, the Trial Chamber found in paragraph 209 that: "The indictment against Dario Kordic is the first in the history of the International Tribunal to allege incitement to hate or encouraging and promoting hatred against a crime against humanity." But the Trial Chamber had found that: "The act, as alleged in the indictment, did not constitute by itself persecution as a crime against humanity, because it was of the view that it is not enumerated as a crime elsewhere in the Statute but most importantly it does not rise to the same level of gravity as the other acts enumerated in Article 5." The Trial Chamber added that: "International customary law does not view this act as a crime, and it would be a violation of the principle of legality to convict the accused for an act under the count of persecution." The legal analysis carried out by the Trial Chamber referred to footnote 272 to the Streicher case and said that the IMT had convicted two accused for persecution because it had "incited the German people to active persecution." The IMT found that the acts of the accused, the publication of a virulently anti-Semitic journal had amounted to "incitement to murder and extermination." Streicher case, IMT judgement, pages 321 to 324. Equally, in the Akayesu judgement, paragraphs 672 to 675, the ICTR found the accused guilty for direct and public incitement to genocide under Article 23(C) of the ICTR Statute. In the Nahimana case, the Appeals Chamber noted in paragraph 979 of the appeals judgement of November 28, 2007, that the submissions of the parties, notably the submission of the amicus curiae, showed that the interpretation of the Streicher case provided by the Trial Chamber was wrong, because, and I quote: "Streicher was for the found guilty of persecution for anti-Semitic writings that significantly pre-dated the extermination of Jews in the 1940s but for prompting to murder and extermination at the time when Jews in the east were being killed under the most horrible conditions." And it further said, and I quote again: "That this interpretation of the Streicher case is confirmed by the fact that the IMT acquitted Hans Fritzsche on the grounds that his hate speeches did not seek incite the Germans to commit atrocities against the conquered people." The Appeals Chamber, for its part, considered that: "The crime of persecution consists of an act or an omission which discriminates in fact and which denies or infringes upon the fundamental right laid down in international customary or treaty law the actus reus of the crime, and was carried out deliberately with the intention to discriminate on one of the listed grounds, specifically race, religion, or politics, the mens rea or -- of the crime." This is in paragraph 985 of the Nahimana appeals judgement. It adds: "However, not every act of discrimination will constitute the crime of persecution. The underlying acts of persecution, whether considered in isolation or in conjunction with other acts must be of a gravity equal to the crimes listed under Article 3 of the Statute." Furthermore, it says that: "It is not necessary that these underlying acts of persecution amount to crimes in international law." On paragraph 986 and 987, the Appeals Chamber goes even further in its analysis, setting there in a very clear fashion once and for all the case law, saying that it considers -- and I quote, and I will read slowly, because this is jurisprudence: "A hate speech targeting a population on the basis of ethnicity or any other discriminatory ground violates the right to respect for human dignity," see the Universal Declaration of the Human Rights, "of the members of the targeted groups, harassment, and is thus a de facto discrimination. In addition, the Appeals Chamber is of the view that speech inciting to violence against the population on the basis of ethnicity or any other discriminatory grounds violates the right to security of the members of the targeted group and therefore constitutes actual discrimination," see Article 3 of the Universal Declaration on Human Rights, "however, the Appeals Chamber is not satisfied that hate speech alone can amount to a violation of the rights to life, freedom, and physical integrity. Thus other peoples need to intervene before such violations can occur. A speech cannot in itself directly kill members of a group, imprison, or physically injure them." Finally regarding the question -- the following question: "Whether the violation of fundamental rights, right to respect for human dignity, right to security is as serious as in the case of the other crimes against humanity enumerated in Article 3 of the Statute. The trial -- the Appeals Chamber is of the view that it is not necessary to decide here whether in themselves mere hate speeches not inciting violence against the members of a group are of a level of gravity equivalent to that for other crimes against humanity, according to which it is not necessary that every individual act underlying the crime of persecution to be of a gravity corresponding to other crimes against humanity. Underlying acts of persecution can be -- can be considered together. It is the cumulative effect of all the underlying acts of the crime of persecution which must reach a level of gravity equivalent to that for other crimes against humanity. Furthermore, the context in which these underlying acts take place is particularly important for the purpose of assessing their gravity." What can I conclude? As far as I'm concerned, I agree with the analysis of the Appeals Chamber, which invites Judges, when they have to make a ruling on the existence of a persecution to review the case in a holistic fashion, drawing their attention to the underlying acts. This cumulative effect could lead to a certain gravity that would make it possible for any reasonable Judge to conclude that there was indeed persecution. But, as far as I'm concerned, this can only be done during final deliberations. Therefore, at this stage of the proceedings, I will not review each underlying act, nor will I assess the entire act in a cumulative fashion as indicated by the Appeals Chamber. At this stage of the proceedings, I will just keep, as underlined by the Appeals Chamber, that discriminatory -- I will only -- I will only keep discriminatory intent as an unlawful ground. This being said, I will now scrutinise and review all the evidence provided by the Prosecution to determine whether there has been discriminatory intent. To do so, I will use a year-to-year approach, year-by-year approach. I will take into account all interviews and statements made by Mr. Seselj in 1990, 1991, 1992, 1993, and I will also mention two of these that are not dated. Thanks to this technique, I will be able to come up with a very clear picture. A number of these elements have already been mentioned in the majority decision, but what's interesting here is to set them in their -- back in their time-frame. I was able to backtrack to June 25, 1990. During an interview at that -- on that day, during an interview with a journalist from "Vecernji List," Mr. Seselj says that the Croats hate the Serbs and that they have megalomaniac ambitions. He adds that hatred is only born to newly created nations. That's Exhibit P1169. A few months later, during an interview to TV Studio B, November 1st, 1990, the accused declares that he is genetically and ethnically Serb. Exhibit P1172. One month later during an interview with a journalist called Miroslav Peranovic, in a Bosnian weekly on December 1st, 1990, the accused declared that the Ustashi movement, so he's now talking about the Ustashi, is a typically fascist movement responsible for having committed a genocide against the Serbian people. Furthermore, according to him, Croatia is a totalitarian state. P1173. And he also advocates the banning of all universities using Siptar language. A few days later during an interview with TV Belgrade on December 6th, 1990, he says except for a very few, Croats are all criminals and should be punished through the loss of hundreds of their territories. P32. Furthermore, he uses the word "Ustashi" several times. Let's now move on to 1991 at the national -- in the parliament on February 23, 1991. He takes the floor, P1255, and says: "We're prepared for a bloodbath." During a speech on television on the network TV "Politika" on April 5th, 1991, Mr. Seselj says that Croats are trying to use the Muslims to pitch them against the Serbs. He says that the creation of a unified Serbian state will make it possible for the Serbian people to have 1.5 million enemies less. And he also says that the Serbs are making one of their biggest mistakes when thinking that Croats are their equals. On May 1st, 1991, in an interview with TV Novi Sad, the accused explains that the revenge of the Serbs against the Croats will result -- revolves the murder of Croatian civilians and that he cannot prevent it. And similarly, according to him, the Serbs cannot be held responsible for this, since, according to him, this revenge is fully justified. P1177. Then we have a video sequence, P1003. I would have -- I almost wanted to show this video, but I think we're running out of time. It's dated May 6th, 1991, and this is what he says: "To our enemies which once again are placing the Ustashi knife under the Serbian throat, we say that we are going to avenge today's victims, but that we are also going to settle old scores." And during a TV interview with TV Novi Sad five days later on May 11th, the accused is ironic in saying that whenever a Chetnik is aiming for a Croat in the head, the Thompson rifles are so effective that their eyes pop out of their orbits. P1254. And on May 24 1991, this is what he says in the news magazine "ON." He says: How can you negotiate with Ustasha? Can't you see that the entire Croatian people is Ustashas except for a very few?" P34. "You know, retaliation results in blind revenge. There will be innocent victims. But what else can be done? The Croats better think twice before doing anything. If they become loyal citizens of Serbia, they will benefit all rights and freedom of -- citizens enjoy, but on the contrary, they'll have to pack and leave." Then on June 1st, 1991, TV Novi Sad, this is what he says -- he seems to boast "for having shed Ustashi blood" in Slavonia. P1180. Then during an electoral speech on June 4th, 1991, this was published in magazine "Horvats Ustasha Phantasmagorias," this is what he says: "If the Croats use you again, the revenge of the Serbs will be terrible, and you will end up way beyond Anatolia." P35. "The Croats are arming themselves. The new Ustasha leader Tudjman today has 80.000 Ustasha commandos armed to the teeth. We told the Croats, 'If you ever engage into a new genocide again, the Serbian people, we will not just avenge each victim, we will use this opportunity to settle old scores in the name of all victims of the two world wars.'" As we see, he's been talking twice about settling scores. Then during a TV interview with Novi Sad on July 25, 1991, the accused says that by nature, Croats are cowards and sent mercenaries rather their armed forces in order to defend their interests. He adds that, according to him, Croats are genetically scared and accuses them of being a criminal people. This is Exhibit P1181. During an interview with a reporter from "Duga," a Serbian bi-monthly on September 13, 1991, the accused suggests that there should be borders, P1182, and he also says, and I quote: "Genetically, Croats are cowards," as he said earlier in Exhibit P34. I would ask our usher to please place on the ELMO P34 and P1182, or -- well, let me ask the Court Registrar to do this. It's done. We have P34 and P1182 in English and also in Mr. Seselj's language. I continue. Speech made before the parliament of the Republic of Serbia on September 26, 1991, and there he calls for the setting up of a temporary Yugoslav government capable, if need be, of setting up a military junta so as to frighten the entire world with these changes. Same session on September 27, 1991, he urges the national -- the parliament to oppose any measure that would result in Serbs living with Croats and Slovenes. P1258. Here I believe that we need to have another document on the ELMO. Very relevant. It's an interview with a journalist of "Ratne Novine," dated November 24, 1991. Here the accused declares the Slovenes as thieves, always deceived the Serbs when the two people -- when these two people cohabited, but you have it here in English. You have it in English and in the language spoken by the accused. Now let's move to 1992. This is an interview with TV "Studio B," April 8, 1992. Here the accused states that he's never in his entire life met a good Croat, and he says that Croats are the Serbs worst enemies. P1195. April 21st, 1992, interview with the "Serbian Daily Unity." Here the accused is calling on their state radios to dismiss all Macedonian, Bulgarian and Croat workers because allegedly they run against the interest of the Serbian people. P1197. A few months later on June 12, 1992, interview with TV "Politika," and there he says that there is no good Croat, neither in Imotski nor in the entire western Herzegovina. P1201. Now let's move to 1993, and here I'm using a press conference which is mentioned in one of Mr. Seselj's books called "The Chief of the General Staff on his knees." Here on -- he says that the SRS has 16 CC-22 rockets, and he threatens to launch them on the Italian civil population should Italy decide to intervene on Serbian land. P1219. I don't know what Italy had to do here, but this is something he said. Then during an interview with a reporter of the weekly "NIN" just one week later, May 21, 1993, the accused says that the worst enemies of the Muslims are the Croats, and here it sounds like fuelling hatred. So after -- I checked all this, but I found two that have no date, but I will still quote them, P1264, P1338, P255, and P256 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you said -- you quoted a statement of mine, and you said that the Croats are the greatest enemies of Muslims. This is how it was translated to me in the Serbian, and this could very well correspond to my words. However, in the translation into English, it says he says that the Muslims are the worst enemies of the Croats. So it's vice versa. The Muslims are the worst enemies of the Croats. But this keeps happening all the time. I took all of the transcripts to check them in French and in English, and there are about 4.000 mistakes of this nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm very happy, because you seem to understand French and English very well, and on the other hand you never want to read any documents in French and English, so I'm very happy to hear this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you from having checked -- having noted this. I hadn't seen this. I was just reading my document and not looking at you sometimes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Lattanzi, I can find my way around in Italian as well, because I used to study Latin and this is how I freshen up my Italian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript has been corrected. This has to be accurate. I know that Mr. Seselj checks everything, and I must not make a mistake, and I endeavour not to make one. This may come from the fact that I read too fast, I don't know. Purportedly said in those unnumbered documents that no crime will remain unpunished, and a sentence which is noteworthy, let me quote: "Hordes of Ustashas have swept over our villages are pouncing on our women and our children and are trying to put an end to the genocide undertaken against the Serbian people." P62. In the Oberschall report, everyone remembers that the Prosecution called Mr. Oberschall as a Prosecution witness for him to testify on the nationalist propaganda of the accused in the 1990s from the -- from 1990 to 1994. The expert, on pages 1822 and 1824 of his report, namely mentions the persecutions, and on pages 9 and following, analyses the speeches on the deportation of the population. Now, to be fair, it is important to remember that on a decision handed down on the 30th of November, 2007, the Trial Chamber dismissed the expert capacity of this witness, but nonetheless admitted for practical reasons his report in it's decision of the 24th of January, 2008. The Chamber will consider the fact that this expert was rejected as an expert to assess the probative value of this piece of evidence, P5. During the testimony of this expert, videos were shown and a number of these videos proved to be particularly relevant as far as persecution is concerned. In video P14, for instance, if we had time we would show it, but we don't have time. This is a speech given by the accused in Jagodnjak in April 1991. The accused mentioned General Tudjman and the new Ustasha authorities, who, according to him, once again held a gun to the head of the Serbian people, and they were once again trying to provoke another genocide. He then declares "each Serbian life will be avenged." In a speech delivered on the 13th of May, 1993, as part of a visit by the SRS leaders in Banja Luka, P18, stated: "The next time they strike, they, the Muslims and the Croat, must be killed so that they never stand up again and that they never strike us again." I shall now more specifically look into the speeches delivered at Hrtkovci. Paragraph 125 of the pre-trial brief considers the statements made by Witnesses VS-26 and VS-1133. According to the Prosecution, these witnesses were telling the truth. However, I must remark that VS-26 ascertains, and he is in total contradiction with the speech delivered by the accused in which he said that "he would gouge out the eyes of the non-Serbs of the Croats and the Hungarians in Subotica with rusty spoons and forks." This does not figure in the speech in question. This same witness said that the accused "met leaders of the SRS and the SUP," and that on that occasion he purportedly called for the deportation and murder of non-Serbs. Witness VS-26, who did not testify for medical reasons, as everybody knows, did, however, testify in the Milosevic case but changed his statement afterwards and wished, despite his poor state of health, to be a Defence witness and stated this on several occasions. Accordingly, as things stand, a reasonable trier of fact cannot accord any credit whatsoever if the statements of this witness are not corroborated by another witness who would then not be challenged. The allegations of Witness VS-1033 [as interpreted], according to which the Accused Seselj purportedly said, let me quote: "Mixed marriages between Serbs and Croats must be purged and the children born of this union must be killed," and he purportedly quoted the personalities of figure-heads that were non-Serbs that should "quitte" Hrtkovci. This has absolutely not been confirmed by the speech which the Chamber has received. In paragraph 127 of the pre-trial brief, the Prosecution holds that the accused delivered a speech on the 6th of May, 1992, in Hrtkovci. And before the speech was given, music was broadcast, and two hours before his arrival, "volunteers of the SRS and the SCP arrived by bus wearing black uniforms and armed with guns." During -- when this speech was given, and I have read this speech over and over again ten times perhaps in order in the to make a mistake, one of the speakers quoted the names of non-Serbs who had left Hrtkovci, and contrary to the Prosecution's allegations, it was not the accused who had quoted the names of these people. All you need to do is look at the documents which the Prosecution has. According to the Prosecution, following this speech, some Croats decided to leave Hrtkovci, relying on VS-1136 [as interpreted] and according to Witness VS-1134, an overall harassment and intimidation campaign had been directed against non-Serbs, and, more specifically, against the Croats in Hrtkovci. These were constantly subjected to threats over the telephone or direct threats. Admittedly the accused did say that no crime would remain unpunished and that the responsible would be taken -- people responsible would be taken to task. These words were uttered in a situation of heightened tension and are mirror words uttered by democratic states nowadays in the event of terrorist attacks, for instance. As the evidence stands and on reviewing the indictment and the trial brief, the exhibits and the witness statements, I can qualify these utterances, interviews, and statements of the accused along the lines of speeches that are likely to be qualified as hate speech and containing a discriminatory ground. Persecution, deportation and forcible transfer. Applicable law. Deportation and forcible transfer of non-Serb civilians, including Croats and Muslims, form the basis of three of the counts mentioned in the indictment. On the one hand, the Prosecution include these crimes under Count 1, persecution. On the other hand, the Prosecution also qualifies deportation as a constituting a crime against humanity, Count 10; an inhumane act constituting a crime against humanity, forcible transfer, Count 11. The Prosecution alleges in paragraph 31 to 33 of the indictment that the accused planned, instigated, committed, or otherwise aided and abetted the planning, preparation, and commission of the crimes of deportation, forcible transfer of non-civilian Serbs, namely Croats and Muslims, between the 1st of August 1991 and the months of May 1992 in the autonomous region of Croatia and the RSK between the 1st of March, 1992, and the end of September 1993 in Bosnia-Herzegovina and between May and August 1992 in certain areas of Vojvodina. The jurisprudence of this Tribunal makes a distinction between deportation punishable under Article 5(D) of the Statute and forcible transfer punishable under Article 5(i) of the Statute under the qualification "other inhumane acts." For those people interested in this question, this distinction was made in the Krstic judgement of the 2nd of August, 2001, in which the Trial Chamber stated in paragraph 521 that: "Both deportation and forcible transfer relate to the involuntary and unlawful evacuation of individuals from the territory in which they reside; yet, the two are not synonymous in customary international law. Deportation presumes transfer beyond state borders, whereas forcible transfer relates to displacements within a state." This distinction, however, does not mean that this should not be unanimously condemned as a practice under international humanitarian law. In addition, jurisprudence has evolved in this respect, and the trans-border nature of transfer has been more closely addressed. The Trial Chamber in the Stakic case held that deportation required the crossing of borders, but this could take on different forms. The Appeals Chamber in its appeal judgement of the 22nd of March, 2006, recalled that international customary law implicitly admits that the victims must be driven out into another country beyond the officially recognised borders and that displacement outside an occupied territory is enough to qualify for deportation. It therefore inferred that "under certain circumstances, displacements beyond the borders could de facto constitute deportation." According to the constant case law of the Tribunal, the material element of deportation is constituted by the facts that people are displaced by force or by some other means of coercion from the area in which they legally reside beyond the official front of a state, or, in certain cases, beyond a de facto frontier in the absence of grounds admitted under international law. However, as far as the mens rea is concerned, the need to prove the intention of the accused to drive out the victims permanently, the jurisprudence of the Tribunal remains unclear. As regards the forced nature of transfer or deportation, it is important to recall the jurisprudence of the Tribunal that this is not restricted to the use of physical forces; that can also involve threat resorting to force or coercion; that it may be in the form of violence duress, detention, psychological pressure, misuse of power; or that it can merely be the consequence of the climate of coercion. And it is only to determine whether the person transferred really had the choice or not. It is important to view this in the light of the circumstances of each case. As far as the lawfulness of transfer of deportation is concerned, the Geneva Convention allow for forced displacement in very specific cases. Article 19 of the third Geneva Convention relating to the treatment of prisoners of war authorise the evacuation of prisoners of war from combat zone in the direction of camps where they will be out of danger. Article 49 of the fourth Geneva Convention on the protection of civilians in wartime authorises a total or partial evacuation of an occupied area, let me quote, "if the security of the population or compelling military reasons so require." That said, the population will have to be brought back home as soon as the hostilities seize in the area. And lastly Article 17 of the second additional protocol admits that the displacement of the civilian population may be ordered for conflict related -- on conflict related grounds. Furthermore, the consent of the displaced people can justify the displacement and make it legal. That said, the consent must be given voluntary and the person must give it of his own free will. In paragraph 17(i) of the indictment, the Accused Seselj is charged with persecution, punishable under Article 5(h) of the Statute for the deportation or trance -- or forcible transfer of tens of thousands of non-Serb civilians including Croats and Muslims, more specifically in Zvornik, in the area of Sarajevo, Mostar, Nevesinje, and in certain areas of Vojvodina. On several occasions, the Trial Chamber admitted that forced displacement of the population constituted persecution. The forced nature of the displacement incur the responsibility of the person committing that act and not the destination or place where these people are sent. This element can be assessed along the same standards as those applied to the crimes of forcible transfer and deportation punishable under Articles 5(d) and 5(i) of the Statute. For the acts of deportation and forcible transfer to be considered as underlying acts to the crime of persecution, they must have been committed separately or accumulatively and have been committed with a discriminatory intent and constitute the crime of prosecution of the same gravity of the other crimes mentioned in Article 5 of the Statute. At this stage, I shall not rule on the question of whether I should expand on the question of deportation or forcible transfer as an underlying act of persecution under Count 1 since I concluded above in light of the evidence received on the existence of Count 1. The essential question which remains is to know whether a public authority may or not call for the displacement of its population. The additional protocol 2 of the Geneva Convention of 1949 relating to the protection of victims during armed -- non-international -- non-international armed conflicts, on 8th of June, 1977, quotes in Article 17: "The displacement of the civilian population cannot be ordered for reasons relating to a conflict otherwise -- unless the security of the civilians or compelling military reasons so require. Should such displacements have to be carried out, all possible measures shall be taken so that the civilian population may be received under satisfactory conditions of shelter, hygiene, health, safety and nutrition. Civilians shall not be compelled to leave their own territory for reasons connected with the conflict." The ICRC commentary in this case says that displacements of the civilian population shall not be ordered unless the security of the civilians so demand or imperative military reasons so demand. Therefore, two exceptional circumstances. I believe that these reasons have to be appraised on a case-by-case basis and that in any event they must be imperative reasons. Therefore, by looking into the speeches as we are going to do in a moment, I did not find in the utterances by the accused either of these two circumstances. Let me now review the evidence on record with regard to transfer and deportation. And as I did before, I'm going to examine the evidence year by year in order to see this inner time-line. 1990. The accused gave an interview to a weekly, the Serb weekly "Pogledi" on the 15th of April, 1990. He calls further displacement of the entire Albanian population living within a 50 kilometre area from the Albanian border to other places in Yugoslavia and recalls that the Albanian ethnic minority, supported by the west, threatens the majority Serb ethnic population. 1991. On the 11th of May, 1991, he gave an interview to TV Novi Sad and said that all the Albanians had to be deported from Serbia. Exhibit P1254.
